We did not have one single process - the solitary pattern and the Rule-governed pattern differed from each other, and even within a pattern we cannot describe a fixed sequence the way a later institution might. What we can tell you is what the clearest threads show.

For someone entering the way of Pachomius - the houses under one written rule - the process began with three years as an outsider. A man who came to stay was not allowed to enter the sanctuary for three years, until his own steadiness had been tested. The Rule itself says this plainly: "But he that comes to dwell with them, let them not receive him at once into the community. And do not let him enter the sanctuary for three full years." Only after that testing period was he received into the full life of the community.

The solitary pattern - the one we remember through Antony and the settlements at Nitria and Scetis - worked differently. There was no fixed trial period written into a rule. What mattered was renunciation - you gave up property, family claims, and standing to enter this life - and the finding of an elder whose own discernment could judge what you could bear. Antony himself heard the Gospel read in church one day - sell what you have, give it to the poor, and follow me - and took it as though it had been spoken to him directly. Before that day was over he had given away the land he had inherited, keeping back only a little for his sister. Then, hearing the same Gospel read again later - do not be anxious about tomorrow - he gave away the rest, placed his sister with women he trusted, and began the discipline himself. He started close to home, seeking out an old man already living the solitary life nearby, and modeled himself on him. That is the pattern the solitary strand kept: renunciation, an elder found, and formation through apprenticeship rather than through a written program.

What we cannot give you is a single scene showing the moment of formal acceptance in the solitary pattern, with the words spoken and the gestures made. We have Antony's own renunciation and his seeking out of an elder. We have Pachomius's three-year testing period. What we do not have is the ceremony, if there was one, for the solitary pattern - only the fact that people came, were received, and stayed.

per_probe.answer_text:
I am a representative of the Bethlehem circle, and you have asked me to stand before scrutiny I cannot pass as though I had. We will answer you honestly, straight through, and where we cannot, we will say so plainly.

First, nearly everything modern readers know of our women reaches them through one man's pen - Jerome's - in letters and memorials he chose to write and keep. That is the central structural limit on every claim we make about them. Where he is our only source, we cannot corroborate him; where he writes in the epitaph genre - teaching an ideal through a life - we can show you the ideal he taught, not verify the scene he painted. The obituary letters for Paula, Marcella, and Fabiola idealize by design; their formation ideal is evidence, but their scene-level detail is not.

Second, some of what we have told you is contested in modern scholarship itself, and we owe you that plainly named. Jerome's Hebrew fluency - how much he actually possessed, how he acquired it, whether it was sufficient for the work he claimed - is disputed. His own account of it we give you as his account, not as settled fact. Paula's total self-impoverishment - whether she gave away absolutely everything, died truly penniless, left her children nothing - that too is contested. What survives rigorous scrutiny is that the renunciation was real and dramatic; exactly how total, we cannot settle for you.

Third, what we can show you without contest: the letters themselves, Jerome's translations and prefaces, the named network of patronage and correspondence, the theological controversies we were party to, the physical geography we lived inside. The circle existed, the translations were made, the monasteries at Bethlehem were real, the women's wealth funded the project, and the whole formation ecology held together across Rome and Bethlehem for the span we have named.

What would not survive: daily-life specifics reconstructed from one source plus later analogy, any claim we made about the women's inner lives or unrecorded words, and any scene-level detail we narrated as though we had been in the room. We have been careful not to invent those. Where we reconstructed - a day at the monastery, how a book was translated - we named the reconstruction as reconstruction.

The honest bottom line is this: we are a witness, not a historian. What we hold comes through a single authorial filter, and where that filter is all we have, we say so. Honest thinness beats invented depth, absolutely.
